Classify a pedon under the Australian Soil Classification

Source: R/key-asc3.R
classify_asc3.Rd

Keys a PedonRecord through the Australian Soil Classification, 3rd edition (Isbell and the National Committee on Soil and Terrain 2021), following the online version with its errata. Experimental: this release keys the 15 orders (the key to soil orders) and the suborders of all of them: the Kurosols, Sodosols, Chromosols, Ferrosols, Dermosols, Kandosols and Vertosols (colour classes, and the Aquic Vertosols), the Organosols (the dominant kind of peat), the Podosols (saturation of the B, sulfuric and hypersulfidic material), the Hydrosols (the setting, then mottling), the Calcarosols (gypsum and the carbonate classes), the Anthroposols (the kind of human-made material), the Arenosols and Tenosols (chernic horizons, bleaching, hard materials within 0.5 m, carbonate, nodules, then colour) and the Rudosols (salinity, gypsum, shells, carbic materials, hard materials, sand, gravel, layers), and the great groups of the Kurosols, Sodosols, Chromosols, Ferrosols, Dermosols and Kandosols (pans in or under the B, structure, plasticity, base status, exchangeable Ca/Mg, ESP and carbonate of the B2 or B2t), the Vertosols (the surface), Calcarosols (what the soil directly overlies, and the B), Podosols (the kinds of Podosol B), Organosols (drainage, acid sulfate materials, carbonate and acidity), Hydrosols (acid sulfate materials, the upper 0.5 m, and the order the soil would key to apart from wetness), Arenosols, Rudosols and Tenosols (what the soil directly overlies, nodular, gypsic and argic horizons, carbonate, texture, gravel); the Anthroposols have none in the text; and the subgroups of the Kurosols, Sodosols and Chromosols (chernic and vertic features, bleaching, ferric and manganic horizons, sodicity of the lower B, mottling of the B2t, base status, carbonate) and of the Dermosols, Kandosols and Ferrosols (the same features read on the B2, a strongly acid B2, argic and bauxitic horizons in the B, a snuffy A), of the Vertosols and Calcarosols (acid sulfate materials, pans, sodicity, acidity, carbonate and mottling of the upper 0.5 m of the solum and below it, subplasticity, surface carbonate), the Podosols (coherence of the B, pans), the Organosols (what the organic materials overlie), and the Hydrosols, Arenosols, Rudosols and Tenosols (peat kinds, sulfidic materials near the surface, acidity and carbonate of the upper 1.0 m, the B, the A2, the solum or the soil, horizons with all but the thickness; the Rudosolic and Tenosolic great groups of the Redoxic and Oxyaquic Hydrosols take the list of the Rudosol or Tenosol suborder the soil keys to apart from wetness). The name is that of the deepest class assigned, in the book's form "Subgroup, Great Group, Suborder Order" ("Bleached, Eutrophic, Red Chromosol"); rsg_or_order keeps the order. With include_family = TRUE the family follows the name as the book writes it ("Bleached, Eutrophic, Red Chromosol; thick, non-gravelly, loamy/clayey, deep"): see classify_asc3_family.

Usage

classify_asc3(
  pedon,
  rules = NULL,
  on_missing = c("warn", "silent", "error"),
  gapfill = FALSE,
  include_family = FALSE
)

Arguments

pedon

A PedonRecord.

rules

Optional pre-loaded rule set (load_rules("asc3")).

on_missing

One of "warn" (default), "silent", "error".

gapfill

Opt-in within-pedon gap-fill, as in classify_usda.

include_family

Derive the family (classify_asc3_family) and write it after the name. Default FALSE (the result is as in earlier versions).

Value

A ClassificationResult with system_id "asc3", the deepest class in name, the order in rsg_or_order, the classes of each level in levels, the key trace, and provisional_because (classes before the assigned ones that could not be decided); with include_family, the family criteria in trace$family, their names in trace$family_label and their codes in trace$family_code.

Details

The ASC is largely morphological. The diagnostics read field texture grades (field_texture, NCST Field Handbook codes; lab clay stands in and is undecided near the limits), the Australian horizon notation (A1, A2, B21t, Bhs, Bk ...; FAO/USDA designations are read by the role of each horizon), the boundary between the A and the B, pH (strongly acid: pHw below 5.5), ESP (sodic: 6 or more), subplasticity, free iron, grade of pedality, carbonates and the moisture of the horizons when described (soil_water_status: the Vertosols' cracks are not required in a solum described moist), mottles, soft and hard carbonate, gypsum, the kind of peat, acid sulfate tests, EC of a 1:5 extract, dry and moist strength, ped size, nodules, pans and exchangeable bases. From the site it reads drainage_class (Hydrosols, organic materials, Podosol suborders), tidal_inundation (Hydrosols, organic materials), surface_condition (a cracking surface, Vertosols; a saline one, Salic Hydrosols), landform, landform_element, tidal_zone, subaqueous and salinised (Hydrosol suborders) and designation_system ("asc" for the Australian notation). The choices where the text is silent are listed in system.file("rules", "asc3", "readings.yaml", package = "soilKey").

References

Isbell, R.F. and the National Committee on Soil and Terrain (2021). The Australian Soil Classification, 3rd ed. CSIRO Publishing, Melbourne. Online version: www.soilscienceaustralia.org.au/asc.

See also

make_asc3_example, classify_asc3_family, soilkey_systems.

Examples

res <- classify_asc3(make_asc3_example("chromosols"), on_missing = "silent")
res$name
#> [1] "Bleached, Eutrophic, Red Chromosol"
classify_asc3(make_asc3_example("chromosols"), on_missing = "silent",
              include_family = TRUE)$name
#> [1] "Bleached, Eutrophic, Red Chromosol; thick, non-gravelly, loamy/clayey, deep"
